scenes.tts: Why would a healthy ear send sound back out? And what can a screening test learn from it?
scenes.visual: Title card: The Sound That Comes Back. The sealed ear canal and microphone from the start of the lesson.
scenes.narration: Why would a healthy ear send sound back out? And what can a screening test learn from it?

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-eight, Kemp played brief clicks into human ear canals and averaged the response.
scenes.caption: In 1978, Kemp played brief clicks into human ear canals and averaged the response.
scenes.visual: A click enters the canal; many traces stack and average. Label: Kemp, 1978.
scenes.narration: In 1978, Kemp played brief clicks into human ear canals and averaged the response.

scenes.tts: A slowly decaying sound remained after each click. In the ears tested with cochlear deafness, it was absent.
scenes.visual: The averaged trace: the click, then a slowly decaying tail after 5 ms. A second trace, ear with cochlear deafness, flat.
scenes.narration: A slowly decaying sound remained after each click. In the ears tested with cochlear deafness, it was absent.

scenes.tts: Some emissions come from reflections of the travelling wave. Others come from the cochlea's nonlinearity.
scenes.visual: Two labelled boxes: reflection (click-evoked); nonlinearity (distortion product).
scenes.narration: Some emissions come from reflections of the travelling wave. Others come from the cochlea's nonlinearity.

scenes.tts: Picture a curve that acts on the sound wave instant by instant. It passes small inputs and flattens large ones. Feed it two tones, at two thousand and twenty-four hundred hertz.
scenes.visual: An input-output curve: straight near the origin, flattening at large inputs. Label: toy fast nonlinearity. Two spectral bars, at 2,000 and 2,400 Hz, enter the curve.
scenes.narration: Picture a curve that acts on the sound wave instant by instant. It passes small inputs and flattens large ones. Feed it two tones, at 2,000 and 2,400 hertz.
scenes.caption: Picture a curve that acts on the sound wave instant by instant. It passes small inputs and flattens large ones. Feed it two tones, at 2,000 and 2,400 hertz.

scenes.tts: Predict. What comes out, besides the two tones you put in?
scenes.visual: The output spectrum is blank except for a question mark. Text: Predict.
scenes.narration: Predict. What comes out, besides the two tones you put in?

scenes.tts: New tones. Where the two tones add up to a big peak, the curve squashes it.
scenes.visual: The summed waveform passes through the curve; its tallest peaks are flattened.
scenes.narration: New tones. Where the two tones add up to a big peak, the curve squashes it.

scenes.tts: A cubic term mixes two of the first tone with one of the second. That makes sixteen hundred hertz, among other new tones. In ear-canal tests, that one is usually the largest.
scenes.caption: A cubic term mixes two of the first tone with one of the second. That makes 1,600 hertz, among other new tones. In ear-canal tests, that one is usually the largest.
scenes.visual: Out of the toy curve come the two bars plus new bars: equal small bars at 1,600 Hz (2f1 - f2) and 2,800 Hz (2f2 - f1), and further small bars off to the right (sum products and harmonics). On screen: y = ax - bx^3; 2f1 - f2 = 2 x 2,000 - 2,400 = 1,600 Hz. Then the curve toggles to a straight line and the new bars vanish; label: linear gives back only f1 and f2. Then a separate panel, labelled schematic ear-canal spectrum: generation, cochlear filtering and transmission shape relative sizes; here the 1,600 Hz bar is the most prominent product.
scenes.narration: A cubic term mixes two of the first tone with one of the second. That makes 1,600 hertz, among other new tones. In ear-canal tests, that one is usually the largest.

scenes.tts: Predict again. Play the same tones at a moderate level into a cochlea after death. What comes back?
scenes.visual: A grey cochlea icon labelled after death. Output spectrum with a question mark at 1,600 Hz.
scenes.narration: Predict again. Play the same tones at a moderate level into a cochlea after death. What comes back?

scenes.tts: Usually little or nothing, at these levels. The living drive and amplification are gone. That does not mean every nonlinearity in the transduction channel has vanished.
scenes.visual: The cochlea icon turns grey, labelled after death. The mechanical and electrical drive arrows shrink, and the 1,600 Hz bar shrinks to tiny or gone. The transduction channel's transfer curve stays curved, not straightened. Label: drive and amplification lost; some nonlinearity can remain.
scenes.narration: Usually little or nothing, at these levels. The living drive and amplification are gone. That does not mean every nonlinearity in the transduction channel has vanished.

scenes.tts: That is the one idea at work. The same vulnerable process gives the gain and makes the emission.
scenes.visual: The living and dead curves from chapter one return; an arrow from the shaded gain to the emission bar.
scenes.narration: That is the one idea at work. The same vulnerable process gives the gain and makes the emission.

scenes.tts: A fast, saturating curve makes new tones whenever the input reaches its curved part. What ties this one to outer hair cells is that, at screening levels, it fails when they fail.
scenes.visual: Two notes: maths alone, an instantaneous nonlinearity mixes tones when the input reaches its nonlinear range; the link to outer hair cells, at screening levels it fails when they fail.
scenes.narration: A fast, saturating curve makes new tones whenever the input reaches its curved part. What ties this one to outer hair cells is that, at screening levels, it fails when they fail.

scenes.tts: Newborn screening uses emissions. A pass shows outer hair cells can make an emission through the middle ear.
scenes.visual: A newborn screening probe in an ear canal. A two-box diagram: outer hair cells, then nerve; a check on the first box.
scenes.narration: Newborn screening uses emissions. A pass shows outer hair cells can make an emission through the middle ear.

scenes.tts: It does not show intact hearing. In auditory neuropathy, the brainstem response can be absent or very abnormal.
scenes.visual: A question mark on the nerve box. Labels: auditory neuropathy; emission, outer hair cells; brainstem response, nerve and pathway.
scenes.narration: It does not show intact hearing. In auditory neuropathy, the brainstem response can be absent or very abnormal.

scenes.tts: One question stays open. How far along the cochlea is the gain gathered? A second tone can lower the response to a first one. Changing its frequency changes where it acts, which helps map the gain.
scenes.visual: The uncoiled strip, a measured site marked. Overlapping excitation envelopes for several suppressor frequencies spread along the strip; beside them, the probe response at the site dims for the envelopes that reach nearby.
scenes.narration: One question stays open. How far along the cochlea is the gain gathered? A second tone can lower the response to a first one. Changing its frequency changes where it acts, which helps map the gain.

scenes.tts: Take this with you. A living cochlea's nonlinearity makes new tones, and a microphone in the ear canal can hear them.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: two primary tones in; several distortion products made; the microphone in the ear canal picks out one of them, 2f1 - f2 at 1,600 Hz.
scenes.narration: Take this with you. A living cochlea's nonlinearity makes new tones, and a microphone in the ear canal can hear them.
